explicit_propositions.text: Medicare is a government health insurance program.
Medicare was signed into law by President Johnson on July 30, 1965.
Medicare Part A covers hospital, inpatient, skilled nursing, and hospice services.
Medicare Part B covers outpatient care, office visits, and professional-administered prescription drugs.
Medicare Part C refers to Medicare Advantage plans offered by private insurers.
Medicare Part D provides prescription drug coverage.
The 'donut hole' in Medicare Part D refers to a gap in drug coverage before catastrophic coverage kicks in.
In 2020, the Medicare Part D donut hole was eliminated, reducing patient cost burden.
Medigap plans are private insurance policies that cover out-of-pocket costs not covered by original Medicare.
Approximately 60 million people in the U.S. are enrolled in Medicare, including 8 million under age 65.

assumptions.text: Government-provided health insurance is morally acceptable when aligned with Catholic values regarding care for the vulnerable.
Longevity increases and declining birth rates create unsustainable fiscal pressures on entitlement programs like Medicare.
Public trust in government institutions depends on visible outcomes like equitable access and reduced administrative complexity.
Incremental reforms are preferable to systemic overhauls because they preserve stability and avoid unintended consequences.
Healthcare access is a moral imperative requiring proactive governmental intervention to protect the poor and elderly.
Private insurers can deliver value in healthcare delivery when properly regulated and accountable.
Veterans deserve specialized, accessible, and dignified healthcare due to their service and sacrifice.
Preventative care and early intervention yield superior societal returns compared to reactive treatment models.
Cultural narratives around masculinity and stoicism hinder honest discourse on mental health, especially among veterans.
Bipartisan cooperation on healthcare is possible and desirable, even amid deep ideological divides.
